messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark was forty-six, a graphic designer living in a quiet suburb with his wife, when a routine traffic stop two years ago upended everything. He had been driving home late from a client meeting, his mind still on kerning and color palettes, when the flashing lights appeared behind him. The officer approached, asked for his license, and within seconds the tone shifted. Mark could not remember exactly what he said or did—something about reaching for his registration in the glove box—but suddenly he was on the ground, his face pressed against the asphalt, a knee grinding into his back, his wrist twisted behind him in handcuffs. The officer shouted, but the words were a blur of threat and accusation. He spent the night in a holding cell, charged with resisting arrest, only to have the charges dropped the next morning. No apology. No explanation. The bruises on his ribs and the raw scrapes on his cheekbones took weeks to fade, but the sense of helplessness and injustice never left.

In the months that followed, Mark found that certain things could yank him back into that night without warning. A patrol car idling at a traffic light would send his heart into a sprint, his eyes darting for exit routes before he could think. The sight of anyone with visible injuries—a child with a bandaged arm, a jogger with a scraped knee—was worse: the memory would slam into him whole, the taste of concrete on his tongue, the weight of the officer’s knee pressing down again, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing, overwhelmed and unable to speak. Even his own thoughts turned against him. Unwanted images of the event intruded during quiet moments at his drafting table, and he soon learned to keep his mind occupied constantly—scrolling through social media, playing puzzle games on his phone, any mental noise to drown out the images. When colleagues at his design studio mentioned a news story about police, he excused himself to the restroom and spent ten minutes staring at the tiles, planning how he could slip out of the building unseen if anyone ever came for him.

He began to avoid other people entirely. Lunch invitations were declined, client meetings taken remotely, social gatherings with his wife’s friends refused until she stopped asking. At home, he retreated to the spare room with his phone, burning hours on online games and endlessly refreshing news feeds. The distraction worked for a few minutes, but then a notification sound or a sudden noise from the kitchen would flash the memory back, and he would feel his body tense, muscles locked, ready to run even though he knew—logically—that no danger existed. He could not relax in any room without first scanning for exits, and he came to believe that his life had been destroyed by that one night, that everything meaningful had drained away. This constant scanning kept his body in a state of high alert, and because no attack ever came, his nervous system interpreted the absence of danger as proof that he had successfully prepared, not that there was no threat to begin with. What happened to him was deeply unfair, he was certain of that, and nothing had been done about it—no one had been held accountable, no apology offered, no system corrected. That conviction fed a constant low-grade vigilance, a feeling that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he must always be ready. On days when that vigilance was highest, the memory would surface without warning — as if the alertness itself had opened the door. Because he now believed the world was fundamentally unsafe, any hint of authority or sudden movement could confirm it — a police car in the distance, a raised voice in a store, the flash of blue lights on a television screen all became signals he could not ignore.

The memory itself was strange: when he tried to tell his wife what had happened, the words tangled and he lost the thread mid-sentence, the emotion swallowing the narrative. He would stare at her, overwhelmed, and then give up, which only deepened the sense that the event had taken something irreplaceable from him. The more he tried to push the memory away with screens and solitude, the more it ambushed him—while walking the dog, while brushing his teeth, triggered by nothing he could identify. His wife eventually found him one evening in the dark of the spare room, phone glowing in his hand, his face blank. She asked him to talk to someone. He agreed, not because he hoped for change, but because he was exhausted and could no longer see any other way forward than to keep holding still, waiting for the next flash of blue light. This belief that he was permanently damaged kept pulling his mind back to the event, as if he needed to look at it again to measure exactly what had been taken. Each place he avoided became a reminder in itself — the coffee shop he no longer visited, the route he wouldn't take — and the avoidance kept the memory alive.
